entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8057"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 5</title> <div sID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1-Eccl.5.20">Ec 5:1-20</reference>.<div eID="gen12516" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12517" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8057"/>1. From vanity connected with kings, he passes to vanities (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ec 5:7</reference>) which may be fallen into in serving the King of kings, even by those who, convinced of the vanity of the creature, wish to worship the Creator.<div eID="gen12517" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12518" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Keep thy foot--</hi>In going to worship, go with considerate, circumspect, reverent feeling. The allusion is to the taking off the shoes, or sandals, in entering a temple (<reference osisRef="Exod.3.5">Ex 3:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.5.15">Jos 5:15</reference>, which passages perhaps gave rise to the custom). Weiss needlessly reads, "Keep thy feast days" (<reference osisRef="Exod.23.14">Ex 23:14</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.23.17">17</reference>; the three great feasts).<div eID="gen12518" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12519" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">hear--</hi>rather, "To be ready (to draw nigh with the desire) to hear (obey) is a better sacrifice than the offering of fools" [Holden]. (Vulgate; Syriac). (<reference osisRef="Ps.51.16">Psa 51:16</reference>, <reference osisRef="Ps.51.17">17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Prov.21.3">Pr 21:3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.6.20">Jr 6:20</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.7.21-Jer.7.23">7:21-23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Jer.14.12">14:12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Amos.5.21-Amos.5.24">Am 5:21-24</reference>). The warning is against mere ceremonial self-righteousness, as in <reference osisRef="Eccl.7.12">Ec 7:12</reference>. Obedience is the spirit of the law's requirements (<reference osisRef="Deut.10.12">De 10:12</reference>). Solomon sorrowfully looks back on his own neglect of this (compare <reference osisRef="1Kgs.8.63">1Ki 8:63</reference> with <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.4">Ec 11:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.11.6">6</reference>). Positive precepts of God must be kept, but will not stand instead of obedience to His moral precepts. The last provided no sacrifice for wilful sin (<reference osisRef="Num.15.30">Nu 15:30</reference>, <reference osisRef="Num.15.31">31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.10.26-Heb.10.29">He 10:26-29</reference>). <div eID="gen12519" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: CHAPTER 5 Ec 5:1-20 . 1. From vanity connected with kings, he passes to vanities ( Ec 5:7 ) which may be fallen into in serving the King of kings, even by those who, convinced of the vanity of the creature, wish to worship the Creator. Keep thy foot-- In going to worship, go with considerate, circumspect, reverent feeling. The allusion is to the taking off the shoes, or sandals, in entering a temple ( Ex 3:5 ; Jos 5:15 , which passages perhaps gave rise to the custom). Weiss needlessly reads, "Keep thy feast days" ( Ex 23:14 , 17 ; the three great feasts). hear-- rather, "To be ready (to draw nigh with the desire) to hear (obey) is a better sacrifice than the offering of fools" [Holden]. (Vulgate; Syriac). ( Psa 51:16 , 17 ; Pr 21:3 ; Jr 6:20 ; 7:21-23 ; 14:12 ; Am 5:21-24 ). The warning is against mere ceremonial self-righteousness, as in Ec 7:12 . Obedience is the spirit of the law's requirements ( De 10:12 ). Solomon sorrowfully looks back on his own neglect of this (compare 1Ki 8:63 with Ec 11:4 , 6 ). Positive precepts of God must be kept, but will not stand instead of obedience to His moral precepts. The last provided no sacrifice for wilful sin ( Nu 15:30 , 31 ; He 10:26-29 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8059"/><div sID="gen12522" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8059"/>3. As much "business," engrossing the mind, gives birth to incoherent "dreams," so many words, uttered inconsiderately in prayer, give birth to and betray "a fool's speech" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.10.14">Ec 10:14</reference>), [Holden and Weiss]. But <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.7">Ec 5:7</reference> implies that the "dream" is not a comparison, but the vain thoughts of the fool (sinner, <reference osisRef="Ps.73.20">Psa 73:20</reference>), arising from multiplicity of (worldly) "business." His "dream" is that God hears him for his much speaking (<reference osisRef="Matt.6.7">Mt 6:7</reference>), independently of the frame of mind [English Version and Maurer].<div eID="gen12522" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12523" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">fool's voice--</hi>answers to "dream" in the parallel; it comes by the many "words" flowing from the fool's "dream." <div eID="gen12523" type="x-p"/>

When thou vowest a vow unto God--</hi>Hasty words in prayer (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.2">Ec 5:2</reference>, <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.3">3</reference>) suggest the subject of hasty vows. A vow should not be hastily made (<reference osisRef="Judg.11.35">Jud 11:35</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Sam.14.24">1Sa 14:24</reference>). When made, it must be kept (<reference osisRef="Ps.76.11">Psa 76:11</reference>), even as God keeps His word to us (<reference osisRef="Exod.12.41">Ex 12:41</reference>, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.51">51</reference>; <reference osisRef="Josh.21.45">Jos 21:45</reference>). <div eID="gen12524" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 4. When thou vowest a vow unto God-- Hasty words in prayer ( Ec 5:2 , 3 ) suggest the subject of hasty vows. A vow should not be hastily made ( Jud 11:35 ; 1Sa 14:24 ). When made, it must be kept ( Psa 76:11 ), even as God keeps His word to us ( Ex 12:41 , 51 ; Jos 21:45 ).

<div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8062"/><div sID="gen12526" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8062"/><hi type="bold">6. thy flesh--</hi>Vow not with "thy mouth" a vow (for example, fasting), which the lusts of the flesh ("body," <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.3">Ec 2:3</reference>, Margin) may tempt thee to break (<reference osisRef="Prov.20.25">Pr 20:25</reference>).<div eID="gen12526" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12527" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">angel--</hi>the "messenger" of God (<reference osisRef="Job.33.23">Job 33:23</reference>); minister (<reference osisRef="Rev.1.20">Re 1:20</reference>); that is, the priest (Mal 2:7) "before" whom a breach of a vow was to be confessed (<reference osisRef="Lev.5.4">Le 5:4</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.5.5">5</reference>). We, Christians, in our vows (for example, at baptism, the Lord's Supper, &c.) vow in the presence of Jesus Christ, "the angel of the covenant" (Mal 3:1), and of ministering angels as witnesses (<reference osisRef="1Cor.11.10">1Co 11:10</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.21">1Ti 5:21</reference>). Extenuate not any breach of them as a slight error. <div eID="gen12527" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8064"/><div sID="gen12529" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8064"/>8. As in <reference osisRef="Eccl.3.16">Ec 3:16</reference>, so here the difficulty suggests itself. If God is so exact in even punishing hasty words (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.1-Eccl.5.6">Ec 5:1-6</reference>), why does He allow gross injustice? In the remote "provinces," the "poor" often had to put themselves for protection from the inroads of Philistines, &c., under chieftains, who oppressed them even in Solomon's reign (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.12.4">1Ki 12:4</reference>).<div eID="gen12529" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12530" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the matter--</hi>literally, "the pleasure," or purpose (<reference osisRef="Isa.53.10">Is 53:10</reference>). Marvel not at this dispensation of God's will, as if He had abandoned the world. Nay, there is coming a capital judgment at last, and an earnest of it in partial punishments of sinners meanwhile.<div eID="gen12530" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12531" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">higher than the highest--</hi>(<reference osisRef="Dan.7.18">Da 7:18</reference>).<div eID="gen12531" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12532" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">regardeth--</hi>(<reference osisRef="2Chr.16.9">2Ch 16:9</reference>).<div eID="gen12532" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12533" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there be higher--</hi>plural, that is, the three persons of the Godhead, or else, "regardeth not only the 'highest' kings, than whom He 'is higher,' but even the petty tyrants of the provinces, namely, the high ones who are above them" (the poor) [Weiss]. <div eID="gen12533" type="x-p"/>

Proofs of God's judgments even in this world (<reference osisRef="Prov.11.31">Pr 11:31</reference>). The rich oppressor's wealth provokes enemies, robbers, &c. entries.content_plain: 18. Returns to the sentiment ( Ec 3:12 , 13, 22); translate: "Behold the good which I have seen, and which is becoming" (in a man). which God giveth-- namely, both the good of his labor and his life. his portion-- legitimately. It is God's gift that makes it so when regarded as such. Such a one will use, not abuse, earthly things ( 1Co 7:31 ). Opposed to the anxious life of the covetous ( Ec 5:10 , 17 ).

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8073"/><div sID="gen12549" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8073"/>19. As <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.18">Ec 5:18</reference> refers to the "laboring" man (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.12">Ec 5:12</reference>), so <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.19">Ec 5:19</reference> to the "rich" man, who gets wealth not by "oppression" (<reference osisRef="Eccl.5.8">Ec 5:8</reference>), but by "God's gift." He is distinguished also from the "rich" man (<reference osisRef="Eccl.6.2">Ec 6:2</reference>) in having received by God's gift not only "wealth," but also "power to eat thereof," which that one has not.<div eID="gen12549" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12550" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to take his portion--</hi>limits him to the lawful use of wealth, not keeping back from God His portion while enjoying his own. <div eID="gen12550" type="x-p"/>
entries.content_plain: 19. As Ec 5:18 refers to the "laboring" man ( Ec 5:12 ), so Ec 5:19 to the "rich" man, who gets wealth not by "oppression" ( Ec 5:8 ), but by "God's gift." He is distinguished also from the "rich" man ( Ec 6:2 ) in having received by God's gift not only "wealth," but also "power to eat thereof," which that one has not. to take his portion-- limits him to the lawful use of wealth, not keeping back from God His portion while enjoying his own.

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv8074"/><div sID="gen12551" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv8074"/>20. He will not remember much, looking back with disappointment, as the ungodly do (<reference osisRef="Eccl.2.11">Ec 2:11</reference>), on the days of his life.<div eID="gen12551" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen12552" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">answereth ... in the joy--</hi>God answers his prayers in giving him "power" to enjoy his blessings. Gesenius and Vulgate translate, "For God (so) occupies him with joy," &c., that he thinks not much of the shortness and sorrows of life. Holden, "Though God gives not much (as to real enjoyment), yet he remembers (with thankfulness) the days; for (he knows) God exercises him by the joy," &c. (tries him by prosperity), so Margin, but English Version is simplest. <chapter eID="Eccl.5"/>
